d.title: Four metrics, and the one that needs ground truth
d.caption: Three of these are **reference-free** — they need only the question, the answer and the context, all of which you already have on every production request. **Context recall is the exception**: it needs ground truth, because asking whether retrieval found *everything* requires knowing what everything was. Which is the natural division: three run continuously on live traffic, one runs on a curated set.

d.title: A faithfulness pipeline that returns only a number has thrown away the useful half
d.caption: The computation extracts claims from the answer and checks each against the context. **Always log which claim was unsupported**, because that is what a person can act on: a score of 0.80 tells you to investigate and the failing claim tells you what to investigate. That is the same argument 8.9 made about agent traces and 6.8 made about production incidents — **the aggregate says something is wrong and the record says what.**

nodes.label: The aggregate says something is wrong

d.title: High faithfulness with low context recall looks like a success
d.caption: The headline metric reads well and the system is failing. **The model is being scrupulously faithful — to context that did not contain the answer.** So the answer is grounded, cited, and wrong. This is 6.7's refund-policy case in metric form: a query retrieved a document genuinely on-topic and genuinely not an answer, and faithfulness rewarded the model for sticking to it. The split is diagnostic precisely because **faithfulness alone cannot distinguish a good answer from a well-grounded irrelevance.**

nodes.label: The model sticks to it faithfully

d.title: Three modes, and why pairwise is more reliable
d.caption: Pointwise gives an absolute number, which is convenient and **requires the judge to hold a stable internal scale across every case** — the thing 9.4 of module 7 showed humans cannot do either. Pairwise asks only which of two is better, the comparison judges are reliable at, and it is what powers MT-Bench and Arena-Hard. Reference-based judging is the most constrained and needs the gold answer that caps your set size.

d.title: Described points turn measurement into classification
d.caption: "Rate helpfulness 1–5" gives the judge **no anchors, so it invents them** — and invents different ones for different prompts, so the scores drift in a way that looks like signal. Describing what each point means makes the task closer to **classification than to measurement**, which models do far better. It also makes disagreements auditable: if you disagree with a 3, there is a written definition of 3 to disagree with.

d.title: G-Eval removes a quantisation problem that matters more than it sounds
d.caption: A plain rubric judge returns a **discrete** score — 3 or 4, with nothing in between. G-Eval reads the probability the model assigns to each score token and takes the **expected value**, giving 3.4 instead. With a 1–5 scale and a hundred cases, discrete scores give a coarse average dominated by which side of a boundary each case fell on, so two genuinely different systems can produce the same mean. The expectation restores the resolution that rounding threw away.

nodes.label: Each case rounds to a side

d.title: Four biases, each with a mechanical fix
d.caption: None is a reason not to use a judge; each has a fix costing a second call or a preprocessing step. **Position is the one that is free to fix and most often skipped**, and §02 measures what skipping it costs on this judge. Self-preference is the only one that needs a *different judge family* rather than a better prompt — you cannot instruct a model out of preferring its own style.
cells: normalise for length; say to ignore it

d.title: 62% or 53.5%, depending on whether you ran both orders
d.caption: Run only the first ordering and you report **62% — a comfortable win, well clear of a tie, and a defensible basis for shipping.** The order-averaged truth is **53.5%**, close enough to a coin flip that the decision has no support. The **17-point gap is the bias measured on your own judge** rather than assumed from a paper, which is what makes running both orders the highest-value single change available to a pairwise judge: it costs one extra call and it is the difference between a result and an artefact.

d.title: Length is the hack that appears at every layer of the stack
d.caption: 7.11 measured why length is the canonical reward hack: a DPO-style implicit reward is **linear in response length**, so a tiny per-token quality weight is worth as much as the entire quality signal on a long enough answer. 8.3 measured the metric-side version, where a recall-oriented overlap metric gave a perfect score to a longer answer containing the usual phrasing. **Every layer of this stack rewards length for a different reason**, which is why controlling for it has to be done at every layer rather than once.

d.title: More than half of an 80% agreement was free
d.caption: If the judge says PASS 62% of the time and the human 58%, two **independent** raters with those habits would agree on PASS 0.62 × 0.58 = 35.96% of the time by luck alone, plus the matching FAIL term, giving 51.92% expected agreement from nothing. So of the 80% observed, **51.92 points were free**. κ measures what is left: 0.2808 of agreement above chance out of 0.4808 that was available, giving **0.5840**. Raw agreement is not evidence of a working judge.

d.title: The conventional bands, and where 0.584 lands
d.caption: The bands are a convention rather than a theorem, and they are useful for one decision: **whether a judge is good enough to gate on.** 0.584 lands in *moderate*, which means it is usable for tracking a trend and **not** usable as a merge gate on its own — one rater in three disagreeing is too much to block a deploy on. Substantial, above 0.61, is the usual threshold for gating.

d.title: An agent judge sees a different object entirely
d.caption: An answer judge sees a question and a response. An agent judge sees **the whole trace** — which tools were called, with what arguments, in what order, what came back, and how the agent reacted to a failure. That supports judgements an answer judge cannot make: whether the right answer was reached **by luck**, whether a tool error was recovered from or silently swallowed, whether the path was reasonable. None of that is visible in the final string.

nodes.label: An answer judge: question and response
nodes.sub: one string in, one score out

nodes.label: An agent judge: the whole trace
Did it recover from the tool error?

d.title: Seven dimensions, and five of them are free
d.caption: The column that matters operationally is the last one. **Tool selection, efficiency, recovery and cost are all computable from the trace with no judge at all** — they are counting exercises. Only trajectory quality genuinely needs a judge, and tool arguments need one only for the semantic half: schema validity is free. So an agent evaluation suite can be mostly deterministic, which is the opposite of what the phrase "agent-as-a-judge" suggests.
cells: against a gold trace or a judge

d.title: A one-shot success figure on an agent is one draw from a distribution
d.caption: Temperature, tool latency and model non-determinism mean the same input produces **different trajectories**, so a single run is a sample rather than a measurement. 9.7's framing applies directly: report pass@1 and pass@k with **n and temperature attached**, and read the gap between them as an **instability budget**. An agent at pass@1 of 0.70 and pass@5 of 0.95 is not a 70% agent or a 95% agent — it is an agent whose answer depends on the draw, and that is the number to act on.

nodes.label: The gap is an instability budget
And that is the number to act on

d.title: ECE, and a uniform 0.20 shift
d.caption: Bin by stated confidence, take the absolute gap between mean confidence and actual accuracy in each bin, weight by bin size. A well-calibrated model reads **0.0136** with accuracy 0.758 against mean confidence 0.749 — tracking. Shift confidence up by 0.20 and ECE becomes **0.2075**, which is the shift showing up almost exactly: ECE is close to linear in a uniform offset, so the number is readable as "how many points overconfident, on average".

d.title: Refusal has to be measured in both directions
d.caption: A red-team suite measures whether the model does things it should not. **Optimise only that and the trivially best model refuses every request** — it scores perfectly and ships nothing. 7.11 catalogued hedging as the reward hack evaluation misses, because **a refusal is never *wrong* the way an incorrect answer is**, so nothing penalises it. Over-refusal is its safety-flavoured sibling, and the only defence is a second suite of benign requests that *should* be answered.

d.title: Six operational metrics, and the one the user actually feels
d.caption: **TTFT is what the user feels**, and streaming is what makes it the real latency metric rather than total latency. TPOT decides whether the text outruns reading speed — about 25 tokens a second is comfortable, so anything faster is invisible and anything slower is felt as hesitation. And the cost row carries the operative instruction: **multiply by volume before committing to a design**, not after.

d.title: Identical numbers, completely different experience
d.caption: Same TTFT, same TPOT, same total — and streaming changes the product. **With streaming** the user sees text at 400 ms and reads along as it arrives at 40 tokens per second, comfortably above the ~25 they can read. **Without streaming** they stare at a spinner for 5.4 seconds and then receive everything at once. The measurable quantities are equal; what differs is that in the first case the waiting is **filled**, which is why total latency is the wrong headline metric for a chat product.

d.title: A mean of 2 s is consistent with almost anything
d.caption: LLM latency distributions have **long tails** — variable output length, queueing, cache misses, retries — and the mean hides them completely. A mean of 2 seconds is consistent with every request taking 2 seconds and with most taking 1 while one in twenty takes 20. **One in twenty is not an edge case at volume**: at a thousand requests an hour it is fifty people an hour having a bad time, and they are disproportionately the ones who complain and the ones who leave.

d.title: A point estimate without an interval is a coin flip dressed as a decision
d.caption: Every metric in this module produces a point estimate, and **a point estimate without an interval cannot support a decision.** A three-point gap on 200 examples sits well inside a ±5.3-point margin, so the data is consistent with either variant being better — and shipping on it is exactly the phrase: a coin flip dressed as a decision. This is the most common unforced error in the module, and the fix is one line of arithmetic.

d.title: The margin shrinks as the square root, which is the whole problem
d.caption: Four times the examples halves the margin. **50 cases gives ±10.6 points** — enough only to detect a change that is visible by eye. 200 gives ±5.3, and 1,000 gives ±2.4, which is finally fine enough to resolve the kind of improvement a prompt change actually produces. The square-root relationship is why eval sets cannot be cheaply made precise: going from ±2.4 to ±1.2 needs **4,000 cases**, not 2,000.

d.title: Run both variants on the same examples, and the dominant variance disappears
d.caption: Two **independent** runs carry the variance from **example difficulty**, which is usually the dominant source — so you are mostly measuring which sample of questions each variant happened to get. Running both on the same examples and testing the **difference** removes that term entirely. For pass/fail outcomes the right test is **McNemar's**, which looks only at the cases where the two variants disagree — A passed and B failed, against the reverse — and ignores everything they agreed on, which is where the information is.

d.title: Choose by how constrained the output is, not by what is familiar
d.caption: The organising question is **how much freedom the output has**, because that determines what can be checked. One correct answer admits exact match. A reference constrains the space enough for overlap metrics. **Execution is the only row that cannot be argued with** — a test passes or it does not. Retrieval asks whether the answer is *reachable* rather than whether it ranks first. And open-ended prose has no reference, so relative comparison is all that is left.

cells.text: the only one that cannot be argued with

d.title: The pitfalls, by family
d.caption: Each family fails in a way characteristic of what it measures. **n-gram overlap is blind to meaning reversal** — a correct answer in different words scores near zero, and an inverted one can score perfectly. **ROUGE-recall rewards length**, so a summary that copies the source scores well. Judges carry position, verbosity and self-preference. And intrinsic metrics are not comparable across tokenizers or datasets, which is 9.2's three lies.

d.title: A convention trap found by running both halves of the course
d.caption: This module uses linear NDCG gain and module 5 uses exponential — **a discrepancy found by computing both rather than read off a page.** Exponential weights a grade-3 document **seven times** a grade-1 one; linear weights it three times. So "NDCG@6 = 0.96" is not comparable across two teams unless both state the gain function, and the same applies to whether the ideal ranking is built from the judged pool or the full corpus. Two defensible conventions, incomparable numbers, and nothing in the metric's name warns you.
